taxonomyNote: NatureServe's concept includes M. apalachicolae and excludes M. suwanniensis (Taggart and Carr 2025; TTWG 2025); Thomas et al. (2014) had split it into three species.
fieldMarks: Very large: adult carapace usually 38-66 cm (to 80 cm), 16-68 kg; huge head with strongly hooked jaws.
Three pronounced keels on the carapace plus an extra row of scutes along each side of the shell.
Long tail without a saw-toothed mid-dorsal ridge; eyes set more to the sides.
Pink worm-like lure on the tongue.
behavior: Highly aquatic and secretive; leaves water only to nest and occasionally bask; mostly nocturnal or crepuscular.
Lies motionless on the bottom, sometimes algae-covered, and lures fish with its tongue; stays submerged 40-50 minutes.
Eats fish, mollusks, other turtles and other aquatic animals plus carrion.
habitat: Slow, deep water of rivers, sloughs, oxbows, canals and river-connected lakes, also swamps, bayous and ponds; under logjams, undercut banks and in deep holes.
range: Mississippi and Mobile drainage basins and the Gulf Coast from eastern Texas to the Florida panhandle, north to southeastern Kansas, southeastern Iowa, Illinois and southern Indiana; very rare in Kentucky and possibly extirpated in Indiana and Iowa.

lookalikes.name: Common snapping turtle
lookalikes.howToTell: Alligator snapping turtle has a larger head, an extra row of scutes on each side of the shell and lacks the saw-toothed mid-dorsal tail ridge.
